title: Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology?
author: Katie Worth
content:
You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics
and grocery aisles: _“Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.”_ _“Climate pledge
friendly.”_ Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when
companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can
be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away.

Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated
[how the world came to rely so heavily on this
premise](https://www.propublica.org/article/carbon-capture-storage-fossil-
fuel-sally-benson), particularly in the technology known as [carbon capture
and storage](https://projects.propublica.org/why-carbon-capture-cant-solve-
climate-change/). CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be
warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface,
where, ideally, it stays put. The [oil industry has long
favored](https://www.propublica.org/article/wedges-climate-research-bp-fossil-
fuel-princeton) the idea.

At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the
idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.

Over the last two weeks, world leaders and negotiators met in Antalya, Turkey,
for the U.N.’s annual flagship climate summit, where nations hash out global
commitments to curb warming. A central foundation of these negotiations — and
many of those carbon-neutrality labels and climate pledges — is the
expectation that we can bury billions of tons of CO2 a year, an operation that
would rival today’s entire global oil industry within just a couple of
decades.

Yet our reporting found that expectation rests on thin evidence. After three
decades of development, only 12 large-scale geologic storage projects have
ever been built, and at least seven have underperformed or failed. Last year,
the world buried less CO2 underground than a single large power plant emits
annually.

Why do world leaders keep staking climate policy on a technology that remains
unproven?

Because the models they all rely on to guide their approach have already
presumed that it will work.

I spoke to more than 100 experts for this series, including several members of
the wildly powerful group of people who build and run those models. Their
simulations of the economy and environment map out how specific choices, like
retiring coal plants or electrifying vehicles, could prevent warming
catastrophic enough to submerge cities like Miami. Which means that if they’re
wrong, Miami could pay the price.

One [chart laid bare](https://projects.propublica.org/why-carbon-capture-cant-
solve-climate-change/) to me exactly how wrong they’ve been about CCS. It
compares one prominent model’s projections for CCS with their projections for
solar power, a technology so abundantly tested and proven that you can likely
spot a panel out the nearest window:

### Carbon Capture Capacity Has Never Come Close to Projections

Meanwhile, solar electricity production has grown rapidly, far outpacing
projections.

![Two side-by-side line charts show carbon capture capacity and solar
electricity production over time. Each chart contains blue lines representing
projections and a brown line representing real data. In the carbon capture
capacity chart, the projection lines shoot upwards starting in 2020 and
continue to climb through 2040, indicating exponential growth in carbon
capture storage. The brown line labeled “actual carbon storage” stays at just
above zero from 2010 through 2025. In the solar electricity production chart,
the projection lines climb moderately upward from 2010 through 2040, and the
brown line labeled “actual solar electricity production” increases
exponentially between 2015 and 2025, outpacing all of the projection
lines.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261119-ccs-
solar-static.png?w=752)Note: The modeled pathways, what we call projections,
for deployment of carbon capture and storage are from text and tables in the
International Energy Agency’s Energy Technology Perspectives and World Energy
Outlook reports, and from correspondence with the IEA. Lucas
Waldron/ProPublica

I wanted to understand what could possibly account for such a disparity.****
But the problem is the models are opaque: Unlike most scientists, who trade in
public, peer-reviewed studies, modelers aren’t required to document every
[assumption](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1750583622001840#sec0022)
they build into their influential simulations.

So I tracked down the leaders of the world’s three most influential climate
models — one based in the Netherlands, another in Germany and a third in
Austria — and asked. Here’s what I learned:

### Climate models assume it’s easy and efficient to capture carbon. It’s not.

Public data is hard to come by, but
[several](https://ieefa.org/sites/default/files/2024-10/IEEFA%20Carbon%20capture%20and%20storage-
Europe%27s%20climate%20gamble.pdf)
[analyses](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35966457/) [have
found](https://essopenarchive.org/doi/full/10.22541/essoar.15012142/v1) the
real capture rates are far lower than the industry has promised. Yet the
models calculate as much as a 92% success rate. When I pointed out this
discrepancy to Keywan Riahi, who leads the Austrian model, he insisted that
capturing concentrated CO2 from industrial emissions “is not high-tech, this
is very easy to do.” Riahi told me the models assume a high rate of capture
because they factor in incentives such as payouts from carbon taxes and large
government subsidies. Add those incentives, he argues, and the capture rates
would increase.

### They don’t account for problems that come up in real-world practice.

In project after project, operators have struggled to inject as much carbon
into the earth as they say they can. For instance, at Chevron’s Gorgon natural
gas processing plant in Australia, billed as the largest CCS operation on
Earth, clogged wells and pressure spikes have forced operators to release most
of their CO2 straight into the air. As it stands, only the German model, led
by Jessica Strefler, assumed there’d be any limit to how much CO2 operators
could inject underground at once. But, she told me, there is no good data to
work from, and she pegged the limit based on “expert interviews” with people
in the industry.

### They assume the Earth is a bottomless geologic landfill.

Modelers took that cue from a rosy 2005 U.N. report, which I’d learned had
been written at the behest of Saudi Arabia and allied petrostates, that
portrayed underground storage space as practically limitless. (The U.N.’s
climate science body has said it stands by the report. Scientists who
contributed to the report also defended their work. Authors and editors from
Saudi Aramco, Chevron and Shell joined scientists in writing it; the companies
did not respond to requests for comment.) Yet just last year, [a paper in the
journal Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09423-y) warned
that the earth’s capacity to absorb CCS could be far more limited once you
rule out pumping the gas beneath cities, into earthquake zones and under the
deepest parts of the oceans. If CCS ever worked at the scale modelers imagine,
the paper found, the Earth could run out of room as soon as early next
century. Riahi, himself a co-author on that paper, conceded that although his
model presumes the earth’s capacity for carbon storage is literally infinite,
the real potential may be “smaller.”

### They assume that stored CO2 will stay put.

Scientists warn that even tiny annual leak rates over longtime horizons could
undermine a storage site’s climate benefit. Our investigation found two large-
scale sites that have leaked, one all the way to the surface. Surely the
models all factor in this risk? I asked Detlef van Vuuren, leader of the Dutch
model, if his did so. His one-word answer: “Nope.”

### The models all assume CCS gets more affordable over time, though real-
world costs have steadily climbed.

When I asked Strefler if it makes sense to assume our children and
grandchildren will pay big bucks to suck CO2 out of the air, even though today
governments won’t spend pennies to avoid emitting that pollution, she said:
“If a country is not willing to do that, I don’t see how they would be willing
to” pay for CO2 removal.

In short, the modelers overlooked decades of underperformance, inflated
capture rates, evidence of leaks and finite underground storage, all while
assuming future generations will willingly bankroll an increasingly expensive
industry. They pointed to a mix of legitimate studies to support those
assertions. They also pointed to unreviewed white papers, casual chats with
industry insiders and the 2005 U.N. report — of which van Vuuren was an
author. Van Vuuren said his team is working to revise some of its assumptions,
but he generally sees no technical reason why CCS cannot work, or should be
excluded from the possibilities his model considers. He said it is a policy
decision whether countries wish to invest the dollars and effort to make it
happen.  

One way to look at the model projections is as recipes for the future. Seen
this way, the modelers’ argument is that their job is to assemble a cookbook,
not tell us how each recipe tastes. In other words, the models merely show
that if CCS works and is used at an extraordinary scale, it is possible to hit
climate targets. And the modelers told ProPublica and Drilled that the delay
in climate action has left few other tools to do so — and so they include CCS.

A good recipe, though, cannot rely on imaginary ingredients. If we’re making
unrealistic assumptions, why not include the possibility that aliens will
appear and hand us a solution to climate change, I asked Riahi, half joking.

“You can quote me that I think carbon dioxide removal is more likely than an
alien,” Riahi said.

### Note on Data Sources for the Charts

The [2008](https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-technology-perspectives-2008)
and [2010](https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-technology-perspectives-2010)
projections are from the IEA’s Blue Map scenario; a second
[2010](https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/1b090169-1c58-4f5d-9451-ee838f6f00e5/weo2010.pdf)
projection is from the Net Zero by 2050 scenario;
[2018](https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/77ecf96c-5f4b-4d0d-9d93-d81b938217cb/World_Energy_Outlook_2018.pdf)
is from the Sustainable Development scenario; and
[2021](https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/4ed140c1-c3f3-4fd9-acae-789a4e14a23c/WorldEnergyOutlook2021.pdf),
[2022](https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/830fe099-5530-48f2-a7c1-11f35d510983/WorldEnergyOutlook2022.pdf),
[2023](https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/86ede39e-4436-42d7-ba2a-edf61467e070/WorldEnergyOutlook2023.pdf)
and
[2024](https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/140a0470-5b90-4922-a0e9-838b3ac6918c/WorldEnergyOutlook2024.pdf)
are from the Announced Pledges, Stated Policies and Net Zero by 2050
scenarios. Some of these scenarios represent pathways designed to achieve a
specific temperature or concentration of CO2. Other scenarios represent what
is possible based on current policies or pledges. Pathways from years where
underlying data was not provided in the IEA’s report were excluded.

The post [Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture
Technology?](https://www.propublica.org/article/carbon-capture-and-storage-
climate-models) appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
